1:
The opening proposition is read as a doctrine of appointment. Gill takes the season to be a set moment with a set duration, and applies it first to the world itself, which did not exist from everlasting, did not arise from a chance concourse of atoms, and could not have come earlier or later. Wesley adds the qualification the chapter most needs: the verse speaks of a time fixed by God in which things are actually done, not of a time allowed in which they may lawfully be done. Delitzsch finds two ideas in the two Hebrew words — a predetermined time, with its point and its span, and a time suitable to the matter — and praises the Greek for rendering them chronos and kairos, though one ancient commentator drew the distinction too sharply. Ellicott notes that both the word for season and the word for purpose belong to later Hebrew, the latter meaning properly pleasure rather than matter.

Clarke draws two morals before touching the catalogue. The first is that since God assigned particular things to particular seasons, a man who neglects the season sins against providence and authors his own distresses. The second is sharper: God gave man duration, and where nature keeps its course and animals their instincts, man spends his on ends for which no time was ever made, so that of an evil deed nothing can be said but that there was a time in which it was done. He observes that of the whole list only birth and death lie outside human choice, the rest being left to a man's option while still overruled, and reports that Jewish readers find their nation's history in these pairs while others find the church's. He then renders the catalogue as blank verse.

Henry supplies the frame. We live in a world of changes, he says, where the wheel turns and one spoke is uppermost only for a while; since every change is fixed by a power above us, the right posture is neither security nor dejection but an even mind expecting any event. He counts the particulars at twenty-eight, matching the days of the moon's revolution, and notes that some are God's act while others wait on the will of man. Two of his observations have outlived him. There is a time to be born and a time to die, but no time to live, life being too short to mention; and weeping is placed before laughing because we must first sow in tears. On the embracing he is practical rather than conjugal: a friend found faithful is embraced, one found unfair kept at a distance.

Where the pairs are obscure the commentators reach for different keys. Delitzsch refuses to soften killing into wounding, since a man killed can be healed only by resurrection, and insists the author is not ranking these acts morally. Over the stones he wonders about a burial custom before settling on agriculture — stones thrown into a field spoil it, stones gathered out bring it under cultivation — which is Ellicott's reading too, while Gill prefers the ruined temple and the gathering of Gentiles. Both note that the verb rendered lose properly means to destroy and acquired the weaker sense only in later Hebrew, as the Latin word did. Delitzsch also observes that the series ends emphatically on peace, infinitives giving way to nouns at the close. On the question that follows, he hears the complaint of the first chapter returning: nothing produced by labour carries security of lasting. Clarke traces the labour to necessity and then to the basest of passions, concluding that a man who lives without God travails in pain all his days. Henry turns it the other way: the travail is a gift, given as a physician gives medicine, not to make our happiness but to exercise us, this world never having been meant for our rest.
11:
On the beauty of things in their season the group is unanimous, each with his own illustration. Henry insists that what seems most unpleasant is, in its time, entirely becoming — cold is as fitting in winter as heat in summer, night in its turn a black beauty as day is a bright one — and adds the analogy that carries it: while a picture is drawn and a house built we see the beauty of neither, and only the finishing strokes reveal it, so that we who see the middle of God's works cannot judge them. Clarke reaches for the caterpillar, a finished beauty at every stage, and remarks that the most polished works of art are bungling jobs beside the meanest operation of nature. Gill distinguishes what God does immediately, what by instruments, and what he merely permits, finding harmony in all three. Wesley concedes that many events look irregular to a shallow judgment, and defers the verdict until the end is seen.

The next clause is the chapter's crux, and they divide twice over. Ellicott argues lexically that the noun cannot mean world: that sense belongs to post-biblical Hebrew only, and in the three hundred and more places where the word appears in the Old Testament it means eternity or long duration. Reading it so — this being the one place where it carries the article — he sets it against the word for season: life offers alternating conditions, each good in its time, and man misses this because God planted in him a longing for permanence. Clarke reaches the same rendering by another road and turns it positive: God has rooted eternity in every heart, and without it a man could not trace the divine work at all. Henry keeps the traditional world and reports two opposite explanations: that God set the book of the world in men's hearts, giving real capacity to read it, or that men have the world so much in their hearts, so taken up with its cares, that they have neither leisure nor spirit to see God's hand. Wesley takes the first and limits it, some works remaining past finding out.

The advice that follows raises a sharper question of idiom. Delitzsch notes that rendering the phrase as doing good would give the resignation real content, and that the ancient versions took it so; but he follows Ginsburg in objecting that this conclusion is nowhere else moral, and that the next verse assumes enjoyment. He grants that there is no parallel for the phrase meaning to be of good cheer either, and leaves the difficulty standing. Ellicott states the same evidence and comes down for enjoyment, the writer reporting conclusions reached one after another. Clarke and Wesley refuse to choose, taking the verse as advice to use what God gives without harming oneself and to spend it in charity.

The permanence of God's work draws the largest claims here. Delitzsch reads it as a conclusion from experience holding for the future as much as the present, applying to the natural order and to providence alike. Clarke goes further: God has made no being he means finally to destroy, nothing can be added because no new order of creatures will be produced, and nothing taken away because only the power that creates can annihilate. Gill puts it modestly: individuals die while their species remain. On the closing verse Delitzsch renders the last clause as God seeking what has been crowded out, rejecting the version that makes it God seeking the persecuted to comfort them. Ellicott takes it as recalling the past rather than judging it, the writer's subject being the immutable order that repeats itself, though the word chosen leads on to the judgment opening the next section. Clarke, unwilling to stop at cosmology, turns the clause on the reader and asks where the earlier stirrings of the Spirit have gone.
16:
The corruption of the courts is stated flatly and each supplies his own outrage. Delitzsch confines himself to structure, noting the palindrome and canvassing three ways of construing the opening noun. Ellicott names the theme it opens: the imperfection of moral retribution in this life. Gill identifies the courts with the Jewish tribunals, after the older rabbinic reading. Henry supplies the indignation. A judge governed by the laws of religion is God's own deputy, one of those to whom it is said, You are gods; without the fear of God the office is not merely vanity but a lie, and the place that should have been a refuge becomes the prison of oppressed innocence. Better, he adds, that such a people had no judges, and such judges no power. Clarke, who says the complaint has been just in every age, casts his comment as verse and ends with a question the chapter cannot answer: to what asylum shall the injured fly from a tribunal where perverted law acquits the guilty?

The answer offered is a later judgment, and they differ over how firmly it is offered. Delitzsch notices that the righteous are named first, so the verb carries two senses at once — setting a man upright and sentencing the guilty — and stresses that this administration is not immediate but must be waited for. Wesley reads it as consolation reached after grief, and takes that court to examine thoughts and purposes as well as deeds. Clarke gives it an epigram: man has his time below and God his above, where the judged are judged again and iniquity closes her mouth for ever. Ellicott is the most careful. He agrees that a judgment after this life is plainly in view, but insists it is not asserted as a settled conclusion, only as a belief in conflict with the doubts that follow — and points to the formula opening both this verse and the next, which conveys nothing firmer than I thought, and then again I thought.

What follows is the hardest passage here, and the difficulty is whose voice speaks. Gill reports a rendering that would make the wise man quote ordinary speech, impersonating the atheist and the epicure, and rejects it: these are his own sentiments about the human condition. Aben Ezra said the same of the next verse, that it records the thoughts of men who are not wise; Gill declines that too. Clarke escapes by another door, adopting a translation in which the clause becomes a wish — that God would enlighten them and make them see they are like the beasts — and referring the whole to the corrupt magistrates rather than to mankind. Wesley reads it as fact and moral at once: God permits these disorders to show men what they are, and though he made them men they have made themselves beasts. Delitzsch stays with the grammar, deriving the disputed infinitive from a root of cutting and separating, and rendering that God might sift them.

On the comparison itself the group is plain-spoken. Clarke observes that the author moves from great men behaving like beasts to the mortality of bodies in general, and thence by an easy transition to the point of infinite consequence for religion; animal life, he says, is the same in man and beast, both breathe alike, and when respiration stops the animal life is extinguished. He records too that one clause is missing from six manuscripts. Wesley lists the shared diseases and calamities, and adds the limiting phrase the passage needs: there is no pre-eminence in respect of the present life. Ellicott notes that the word rendered breath here is the same as the word for spirit in the verse that follows. Delitzsch spends his note on how three occurrences of one word should be pointed, settling it by manuscript evidence and an older grammarian's testimony.
20:
The common grave is stated without qualification. Delitzsch identifies the one place as the earth, which finally receives every living thing, and distinguishes the two articles in the verse — the first generic, the second pointing back to the dust a man came from. From dust to dust, he says, holds of every corporeal creature; and then he adds the sentence that governs what follows, that it remains possible for the spirit of a dying man to differ from the spirit of a dying beast, but that this is precisely what stands open to question. Gill puts it in five words, the earth from which they came. Clarke turns the whole into verse, where man and the vilest brute draw the same breath, decay alike, and descend to one grave.

Whether the next verse asks a question or makes a statement is the sharpest disagreement in the chapter, and it turns on two Hebrew letters. Delitzsch reports that every ancient translator read them as interrogative, while several modern scholars take them as the article, giving the sense: who knows the spirit of men, the one that goes upward? He rejects that on three grounds — the connection requires a sceptical question, the formula who knoweth leads one to expect an interrogative continuation, and the pronoun in each clause is there only to mark the question. Ellicott agrees, noting that the Greek and a great body of interpreters both ancient and modern render it as a doubt, and that this suits the paragraph: death visibly resolves the bodies of men and animals alike into dust, and if a difference is alleged about their spirits, can it be asserted with the certainty of knowledge? Gill and Wesley take the other side and read the verse as a difference that holds. Gill grants the shared breath and denies the shared spirit, since a man's soul is rational and immortal and returns at death to the God who gave it; Wesley concedes the difference is real and known to good men, but observes that most people never attend to it, their hearts being set on what is present and can be seen. Clarke goes furthest, offering his own translation in which the clauses become assertions — the immortal spirit of the sons of Adam ascending, being from above, and the breath of the cattle going downward to the earth — and pointing out that the same word had meant breath in the previous verse and means spirit here.

The chapter ends by returning to enjoyment, and even here a construction is contested. Delitzsch reports that one scholar, having already rejected the sceptical question, reads the closing clause not as what shall become of a man after his death but as what shall happen after his present condition, and that another follows him in rendering it of the state of the world after his departure; Delitzsch answers that the author had a fitter form of words available for that thought. Gill notes a paraphrase that makes the man rejoice in his good works, and takes it to mean vindication before men rather than justification before God, though he prefers the plainer sense of enjoying the fruit of one's labour and spending it on family and neighbours. Wesley reads the last clause as final: once dead, a man never comes back to see whose hands his estate falls into. Clarke ends where he usually does, in exhortation — do not turn blessings into sin by complaining, since this life is the state in which glory is prepared for, and a man wretched without may still be happy within.
